title: Databases: SQL and theory
description: Write real SQL and run it on a practice database in your browser, then answer the theory questions interviewers ask about transactions, indexes and design.

platforms.name: LeetCode: Database
platforms.note: SQL problems from easy to hard

dataset.title: Practice database: shop and staff
dataset.description:
A small online shop and a company's staff. Dates are text in `YYYY-MM-DD` form (SQLite has no separate date type), so
`strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)` gives the month.

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| `customers` | `id`, `name`, `city` (can be NULL), `country`, `signup_date` |
| `products` | `id`, `name`, `category`, `price` |
| `orders` | `id`, `customer_id`, `order_date`, `status` (`pending`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled`) |
| `order_items` | `order_id`, `product_id`, `quantity` |
| `employees` | `id`, `name`, `department`, `salary`, `manager_id` (NULL for the top manager), `hire_date` |

The line total of an order item is `price * quantity`. This engine is SQLite, so a few functions differ from PostgreSQL or MySQL;
the SQL you write here (joins, grouping, window functions, CTEs) is standard.

questions.title: Customers from India
questions.prompt: Return the `name` and `city` of every customer from India, ordered by name.
questions.solution: SELECT name, city FROM customers WHERE country = 'India' ORDER BY name;
questions.hint: Filter with `WHERE`, sort with `ORDER BY`. Text comparisons are case-sensitive for `=` in most databases.

questions.title: The three priciest products
questions.prompt: Return the `name` and `price` of the 3 most expensive products, the most expensive first.
questions.solution: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3;
questions.hint: `ORDER BY ... DESC` then `LIMIT` (`FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY` in standard SQL).

questions.title: Customers without a city
questions.prompt: Return the `name` of every customer whose city is not known (NULL).
questions.solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL;
questions.hint: `city = NULL` is never true: comparing with NULL gives UNKNOWN. Use `IS NULL`.

questions.title: Countries with several customers
questions.prompt: For each country that has at least 2 customers, return the `country` and the number of customers. Most customers first; break ties by country name.
questions.solution: SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM customers GROUP BY country HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY customers DESC, country;
questions.hint: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after.

questions.title: Orders per status
questions.prompt: Return each order `status` and how many orders have it. Most common status first; break ties by status name.
questions.solution: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY orders DESC, status;

questions.title: Big orders
questions.prompt: For every order whose total is above 100, return the order `id` (as `order_id`) and its `total` (sum of price times quantity). Largest total first; break ties by order id.
questions.solution:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, SUM(p.price * oi.quantity) AS total
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY o.id
HAVING SUM(p.price * oi.quantity) > 100
ORDER BY total DESC, order_id;
questions.hint: Join three tables, group by the order, and filter the groups with `HAVING` (a `WHERE` cannot see an aggregate).

questions.title: Customers who never ordered
questions.prompt: Return the `name` of every customer who has not placed any order, in alphabetical order.
questions.solution:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.name;
questions.hint: A `LEFT JOIN` keeps customers without orders and fills the order columns with NULL. `NOT EXISTS` and `NOT IN` also work; beware `NOT IN` when the subquery can return NULL.

questions.title: Revenue by category
questions.prompt: Looking only at orders with status `delivered`, return each product `category` and its `revenue` (sum of price times quantity), for categories with a revenue above 350. Highest revenue first.
questions.solution:
SELECT p.category, SUM(p.price * oi.quantity) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY p.category
HAVING SUM(p.price * oi.quantity) > 350
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

questions.title: The top spender
questions.prompt: Which customer has spent the most on orders that are not cancelled? Return that customer's `name` and `total`.
questions.solution:
SELECT c.name, SUM(p.price * oi.quantity) AS total
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 1;
questions.hint: Group by the customer (include `c.id`, two customers can share a name), sort by the sum, take one row.

questions.title: Earning more than the manager
questions.prompt: Return the `name` of every employee who earns more than their own manager, in alphabetical order.
questions.solution:
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary
ORDER BY e.name;
questions.hint: Join the table to itself: one copy plays the employee, the other the manager.

questions.title: Above the department average
questions.prompt: Return the `name`, `department` and `salary` of every employee who earns more than the average salary of their own department. Order by department, then by salary highest first.
questions.solution:
SELECT e.name, e.department, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department = e.department)
ORDER BY e.department, e.salary DESC;
questions.hint: A correlated subquery that refers to the outer row, or a join to a per-department average computed in a CTE.

questions.title: Second highest salary
questions.prompt: Return the second highest distinct salary as a single value.
questions.solution: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
questions.hint: The maximum below the maximum. Alternatives: `SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1`, or `DENSE_RANK()`.

questions.title: Top two salaries per department
questions.prompt: For each department, return the employees who have one of the two highest distinct salaries in that department (people with equal salaries share a rank, so a tie can produce more than two rows). Return `name`, `department`, `salary`, ordered by department, salary highest first, then name.
questions.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, department, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
)
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY department, salary DESC, name;
questions.hint: A window function cannot be used in `WHERE` directly, so compute the rank in a CTE or subquery first. `RANK` leaves gaps after ties, `DENSE_RANK` does not.

questions.title: Monthly revenue with a running total
questions.prompt: For delivered orders only, return one row per month with `month` (as `YYYY-MM`), `revenue` for that month, and `running_total`, the revenue of that month plus all earlier months. Oldest month first.
questions.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month, SUM(p.price * oi.quantity) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue, SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running_total
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
questions.hint: Aggregate to one row per month first, then add `SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY month)` on top.

questions.title: Month-over-month change
questions.prompt: Using the same monthly delivered revenue, return `month`, `revenue` and `change`: this month's revenue minus the previous month's (NULL for the first month). Oldest month first.
questions.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month, SUM(p.price * oi.quantity) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
questions.hint: `LAG(column) OVER (ORDER BY ...)` reads the previous row's value.

questions.title: Customers who bought from every category
questions.prompt: Return the `name` of each customer who has bought at least one product from every product category, counting only orders that are not cancelled.
questions.solution:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.category) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT category) FROM products);
questions.hint: This is relational division: compare the number of distinct categories a customer bought with the total number of categories.

questions.title: What does ACID mean?
questions.prompt: Explain each letter of ACID, with one example of what goes wrong without it.
questions.answer:
**Atomicity**: a transaction either happens completely or not at all. Without it, a transfer could debit one account and crash before crediting the other.

**Consistency**: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, so constraints (keys, checks, foreign keys) always hold after commit.

**Isolation**: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work. Without it, one report could read a balance in the middle of another transaction's update.

**Durability**: once committed, the data survives a crash or power loss. Databases achieve it by writing the change to a write-ahead log on disk before acknowledging the commit.

questions.title: Isolation levels and anomalies
questions.prompt: Name the three classic read anomalies and the isolation level that prevents each. Which level does PostgreSQL use by default?
questions.answer:
- **Dirty read**: reading another transaction's uncommitted change. Prevented from READ COMMITTED upwards.
- **Non-repeatable read**: reading the same row twice and getting different values because someone committed in between. Prevented from REPEATABLE READ.
- **Phantom read**: running the same query twice and getting different *sets* of rows because someone inserted or deleted matching rows. Prevented by SERIALIZABLE in the SQL standard (PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ, which is snapshot based, also prevents it).

PostgreSQL and Oracle default to **READ COMMITTED**; MySQL InnoDB defaults to **REPEATABLE READ**. Higher isolation costs more locking or more retries, so choose the lowest level that is correct for the operation.
questions.hint: Think of what each level adds: first no dirty reads, then stable rows, then stable result sets.

questions.title: How does an index help, and when does it not?
questions.prompt: Explain how a B-tree index speeds up queries, and give three cases where a query cannot use an index well.
questions.answer:
A B-tree index keeps the indexed column values in sorted order in a balanced tree, so the database finds a value, a range or the first rows of an `ORDER BY` in O(log n) page reads instead of scanning the whole table. A **composite index** `(a, b)` helps queries that filter on `a`, or on `a` and `b` (the leftmost prefix), but not on `b` alone.

It helps little or not at all when:
1. The column is wrapped in a function or expression: `WHERE LOWER(email) = ...` or `WHERE price + 1 > 10` (use a functional index or rewrite).
2. The pattern starts with a wildcard: `LIKE '%son'` cannot use the sort order.
3. The column has low selectivity (a boolean, a status with 3 values) so the planner prefers a scan, or the query returns a large fraction of the table.

Indexes are not free: each one slows `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` and uses disk and memory. Read the plan with `EXPLAIN` before and after adding one.

questions.title: INNER, LEFT and FULL joins
questions.prompt: What is the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN? What happens to rows with NULL in the join column?
questions.answer:
- **INNER JOIN** returns only the rows that have a match on both sides.
- **LEFT JOIN** returns every row of the left table; where the right table has no match its columns are NULL. Filtering on a right-table column in the `WHERE` clause turns it back into an inner join, so put such conditions in the `ON` clause when you want to keep unmatched rows.
- **FULL OUTER JOIN** returns every row of both tables, with NULLs where there is no match on the other side (not available in MySQL or SQLite older versions).

`NULL = NULL` is not true, so rows with NULL in the join column never match each other in an equi-join.

questions.title: Normalisation
questions.prompt: Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with a short example, and say when you would denormalise on purpose.
questions.answer:
**1NF**: every column holds one atomic value and there are no repeating groups (no `phones = '123, 456'`; use a child table).

**2NF**: in a table with a composite key, every non-key column depends on the *whole* key, not part of it. In `order_items(order_id, product_id, product_name, quantity)` the `product_name` depends only on `product_id`, so it moves to `products`.

**3NF**: non-key columns depend on the key and *nothing but* the key. In `employees(id, department_id, department_name)`, `department_name` depends on `department_id`, so it moves to `departments`.

Normalising removes update anomalies and duplicated data. You denormalise on purpose for read performance (a precomputed `order_total`, a copied `customer_name` on an invoice that must keep the historical value, a reporting table), accepting that you must keep the copies consistent.

questions.title: Slow pagination
questions.prompt: `SELECT ... ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000` gets slower the deeper you page. Why, and what is the alternative?
questions.answer:
With `OFFSET n` the database must still produce and discard the first n rows before returning the next 20, so the cost grows linearly with the page number, and concurrent inserts can make rows move between pages.

**Keyset (seek) pagination** remembers the last key of the previous page and asks for what comes after it: `WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`. With an index on `id` the database jumps straight to the start of the page in O(log n), whatever the depth. For a non-unique sort column, use a composite condition such as `(created_at, id) > (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId)`. The trade-off is that you cannot jump to an arbitrary page number, only move forward and back.

questions.title: Deadlocks
questions.prompt: How does a database deadlock happen, and how do you reduce them in an application?
questions.answer:
A deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs: T1 updates row A then wants row B, while T2 updated row B and wants row A. Neither can proceed. The database detects the cycle and aborts one transaction, which the application sees as an error to retry.

To reduce them: **access rows in the same order** in every transaction (for example by ascending id), **keep transactions short** and avoid user interaction or remote calls inside them, **lock only what you need** (use indexes so updates do not lock whole ranges), use a lower isolation level where it is correct, and **retry** the aborted transaction a bounded number of times.

questions.title: WHERE versus HAVING
questions.prompt: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and in which order does a SELECT logically run?
questions.answer:
`WHERE` filters individual rows **before** grouping, so it cannot use aggregate functions. `HAVING` filters groups **after** `GROUP BY`, so it can (`HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`). Where possible, filter with `WHERE`: it reduces the rows that have to be grouped.

The logical order is: `FROM` and `JOIN`, then `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `SELECT` (computing expressions and aliases), `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, and finally `LIMIT`. That is why a column alias defined in `SELECT` cannot be used in `WHERE` in standard SQL (some databases allow it in `HAVING` or `ORDER BY`).
